questions.why: A sudden focal deficit still present after an hour, with ischaemia on imaging, is a stroke, not a TIA. Earlier brief episodes in the same territory were TIAs and are warnings that need same-day assessment.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman in general practice. Eight-day periods with 2-hourly changes, flooding and clots, a takeaway diet, pallor and koilonychia, Hb 86 with MCV 68, and ferritin 4 with a normal CRP. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Haematological malignancy such as acute leukaemia
notes: No melaena, rectal bleeding, abdominal pain or bowel change, she is 23, and heavy periods fully explain the loss.
White cells are normal, the film shows no blasts, the platelets are raised rather than low, and she has no bruising, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly or fevers.
TSH is normal at 1.6, and she has no weight gain or goitre, so it is not contributing to her fatigue or her heavy bleeding.
questions.why: In fatigue in a young woman, always take a menstrual history: lengthening periods, changes every 2 hours, overnight changes, flooding and clots indicate heavy menstrual bleeding.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man in general practice. A daily bilateral pressing headache of 5 to 6/10 that builds through the day, not worse with cycling, with neck and shoulder stiffness, tender pericranial muscles, thesis stress and long desk hours, and a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Six weeks of daily headache in someone who is well, afebrile, with no rash, photophobia or meningism and full passive neck flexion.
Never on waking, not worse with coughing, straining or lying down, no vomiting, sharp discs with venous pulsations and a normal neurological examination.
The pain is bilateral, pressing and moderate, not throbbing, with no nausea, light or noise sensitivity or aura, and it is not worsened by activity.
questions.why: Separate primary from secondary headache by grouping your red flag questions by diagnosis: SAH (thunderclap onset), meningitis (fever, rash, neck stiffness), raised pressure or tumour (progressive, worst on waking, worse with coughing or straining, vomiting), stroke or TIA, and head injury.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man in the emergency department. Three hours of left-sided pressure to the left arm and jaw with sweating, nausea and breathlessness, hypertension and a father with an MI at 61, ST elevation in V2 to V5, I and aVL with reciprocal depression in III, and a raised troponin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: The pain is a gradual pressure, not tearing, with no back pain, his arm BPs and pulses are equal, and the mediastinum is not widened.
The pain is not pleuritic, he has no travel, immobility or calf symptoms, SpO2 is 96% on room air, and the ECG shows territorial ST elevation.
No viral illness, the pain is not positional or pleuritic, there is no rub, and the ST elevation is territorial with reciprocal depression and Q waves.
questions.why: STEMI is an ECG and clinical diagnosis: ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads (in V2 to V3 at least 2 mm in men 40 or over, 1 mm in other leads) with ischaemic symptoms. Reperfusion never waits for the troponin.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man in general practice. Sudden-onset, self-terminating, fast irregular palpitations now daily, an irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit, an ECG with no P waves, a regular pulse after the episode stopped, and heavy alcohol, smoking, hypertension, OSA and obesity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Narrow QRS complexes, no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting, and no ischaemic change on the ECG.
Sustained fast episodes lasting minutes to hours, and the ECG shows a continuous irregular rhythm without P waves rather than isolated early beats.
The rhythm he taps and the ECG are irregularly irregular, with no regular flutter waves.
questions.why: Ask the patient to tap out the palpitations: fast and irregular points to AF, fast and regular to SVT or VT, and a missed beat to ectopics.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man in the emergency department. Known heart failure with 3 days of worsening exertional breathlessness, 3-pillow orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling and weight gain, a raised JVP, bibasal crackles, NT-proBNP 4800, congestion on X-ray, and 5 days of ibuprofen with creatinine 132 from a baseline of 86. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute decompensated heart failure precipitated by a non-steroidal
Acute coronary syndrome precipitating heart failure
notes: No chest pain, no ischaemic change on the ECG and a normal hs-troponin.
He is anticoagulated with rivaroxaban, the onset was gradual, the leg swelling is symmetrical with soft calves, and congestion explains the picture.
No fever, sputum or URTI symptoms, normal WCC and CRP, and no consolidation on X-ray.
questions.why: Orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling and falling exercise tolerance in someone with known heart failure mean decompensation: quantify the change (pillows, distance walked, weight).

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman in the emergency department. Known asthma, sudden breathlessness while jogging without her pre-exercise reliever, a recent cold, allergen and smoke exposure, wheeze, chest tightness and night cough, atopy, widespread bilateral wheeze and a low pCO2. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Widespread wheeze with an asthma trigger, no pleuritic pain or haemoptysis, no immobility or previous clot, and soft, non-tender calves.
No lip, tongue or throat swelling, no stridor, hives or GI symptoms, and a normal BP.
No pleuritic or one-sided pain, no trauma, a central trachea, and symmetrical resonance and air entry.
questions.why: In acute breathlessness with wheeze, assess severity from speech, accessory muscle use, conscious state and SpO2, and start oxygen and bronchodilators before taking a detailed history.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in the emergency department. Known COPD in a heavy current smoker, with breathlessness worse since last night, wheeze, a new yellow sputum, feeling hot, partial relief from the paramedics' bronchodilator, widespread wheeze, raised WCC and CRP, and hyperinflation with no consolidation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
notes: No pleuritic pain, symmetrical expansion and breath sounds, trachea central, and no pneumothorax on X-ray.
Already anticoagulated with apixaban, no pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility or calf swelling, and a clear infective, wheezy picture.

Tightness is respiratory in character (not crushing, no radiation), ECG sinus tachycardia with no acute change, first hs-troponin below the 99th percentile (repeat pending), no orthopnoea or oedema, JVP not raised, and no oedema on CXR.
questions.why: In a person with COPD, more breathlessness with wheeze and a change in sputum colour or volume is an exacerbation until proven otherwise; actively exclude pneumonia, pneumothorax, PE and cardiac causes in the history, the examination and the X-ray.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man in the emergency department. Previous MI and CABG with hypertension, diabetes and smoking, a month of falling exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, PND, frothy sputum and leg oedema to the knees, a raised JVP with an S3, NT-proBNP 6200 and a chest X-ray showing oedema, bilateral effusions and cardiomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome precipitating heart failure
notes: Chest tightness unlike his MI and non-radiating, no nausea or drenching sweat like his MI, unchanged ECG.
No pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immobility or recent surgery, the leg swelling is symmetrical with soft calves, and heart failure explains the whole picture.
No pleuritic pain or injury, the trachea is central, both bases are dull rather than hyperresonant, and the X-ray shows no pneumothorax.
questions.why: Ask every breathless patient about orthopnoea, PND, frothy sputum, ankle swelling and falling exercise tolerance, and examine the JVP, heart sounds, lung bases and legs.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman in general practice. 50 pack-years, progressive exertional breathlessness, chronic white productive cough, wheeze, flare-ups with colds, hyperinflation with wheeze, and post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.50 with FEV1 58% predicted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No weight loss, appetite change, night sweats, haemoptysis, hoarseness or lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar enlargement on the chest X-ray.
The tightness comes with wheeze and breathlessness, is not crushing, does not radiate and has no sweating or nausea.
Productive rather than dry cough, no fine crackles or clubbing, no interstitial change on X-ray, and obstructive rather than restrictive spirometry.
questions.why: COPD is confirmed on spirometry by a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7; by COPD-X, an FEV1 of 40 to 59% predicted is moderate disease. A chest X-ray supports it and excludes other causes but cannot diagnose it.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in general practice. Lower abdominal pain before bowel motions with urgency, alternating loose and hard stools, bloating, triggers of stress and dairy, gastroenteritis 6 months ago, and normal bloods, coeliac serology, calprotectin and stool tests. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No blood, weight loss, night symptoms or extraintestinal features, no right iliac fossa mass, and a normal CRP and calprotectin of 28.
Aged 26 with no rectal bleeding, weight loss, anaemia or family history, a normal examination and a normal calprotectin.
Negative tTG-IgA with a normal total IgA while eating gluten, and normal ferritin and folate.
questions.why: In chronic lower GI symptoms, screen every patient for red flags: rectal bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, anaemia, fever, a mass, and a family history of colorectal cancer, IBD or coeliac disease. Rectal bleeding with a change in bowel habit warrants colonoscopy even in a young adult.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man in general practice. Sudden productive cough with offensive yellow sputum 2 days after discharge, fevers and rigors, right pleuritic pain, right basal consolidation signs, WCC 16.4 with neutrophilia, CRP 168, and right lower lobe consolidation that was not on the X-ray 8 days ago. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hospital-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe
Acute left heart failure or acute coronary syndrome
notes: He walked daily and had daily prophylactic anticoagulant injections in hospital, has normal calves and no haemoptysis, has a Wells score of 1.5 (HR over 100 only) with a D-dimer below the age-adjusted cut-off, and the X-ray shows a clear alternative.

No pink frothy sputum, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea or oedema, JVP not raised, pleuritic pain unlike the admission pain, ECG with sinus tachycardia and no acute ischaemic change, and normal heart size with no oedema on the X-ray; troponin still to be checked in hospital.
The recent admission is the more likely source; normal sodium and LFTs, with no diarrhoea, headache, confusion or exposure to potting mix, spas or cooling towers, argue against Legionella.
questions.why: Always ask about recent hospital stays in a patient with an acute cough: pneumonia starting soon after discharge may be hospital-acquired, and the stay is also a risk factor for PE.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman in general practice. First episode starting after daily oxycodone with no laxative, hard pebbly stools with straining, faecal loading, hard stool in the rectum and a posterior midline fissure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Postoperative ileus or adhesive small bowel obstruction
notes: Passing wind, no pain or vomiting, a soft non-tender abdomen, normal bowel sounds and normal observations.
Aged 35, acute onset with a clear trigger, no weight loss or family history, a fissure explains the blood, and no rectal mass.
No cold intolerance, weight gain or dry skin, no goitre, and TSH 1.6.
questions.why: New constipation needs a search for what has changed: here, oxycodone and iron after surgery, on a low-fibre diet with less activity.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman in general practice. Months of daytime sleepiness with unrefreshing sleep, chronic heavy snoring, poor concentration, BMI 36 with a 42 cm neck and crowded oropharynx, hypertension, T2DM, smoking, evening alcohol, ESS 15, STOP-Bang 5 and OSA50 6. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No weight loss, night sweats, fevers, lumps or bleeding, and a normal blood count.
No cold intolerance, constipation or skin changes, normal reflexes and a normal TSH.
Regular periods and no hot flushes or night sweats.
questions.why: Separate sleepiness (dozing off) from fatigue (lack of energy) early. Sleepiness points to a sleep disorder such as OSA.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man in the emergency department. A minor fall hitting the right side of his head 5 days ago, then 3 days of progressive right-sided headache on apixaban, now drowsier; crescentic mixed-density right collection crossing sutures with 8 mm midline shift. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No loss of consciousness or lucid interval, no skull fracture, and the collection is crescentic and crosses the suture lines.
Gradual onset over days with no thunderclap, no neck stiffness or photophobia, and no subarachnoid blood on CT.
Clear history of head trauma, no morning or postural features or weight loss, and no mass on CT.
questions.why: In every older person with a new or progressive headache, ask directly about falls or head injury and about anticoagulants. A trivial knock days earlier, with no loss of consciousness, is the typical story for a subdural haematoma.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old man in general practice. Progressive jaundice with dark urine, pale stools, pain radiating to the back, weight loss, smoking since 15, diabetes from age 75, CA 19-9 of 1,240 and a pancreatic head mass with a double duct sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma causing obstructive jaundice
notes: The mass is centred in the pancreatic head with pancreatic duct dilatation and body and tail atrophy.
The obstruction ends at a pancreatic head mass and the course is progressive with weight loss; no stone is seen, though CT can miss stones.
Surgery was 10 years ago and the duct ends at a pancreatic head mass.
questions.why: Dark urine, pale stools and a cholestatic LFT pattern (conjugated bilirubin, ALP and GGT raised more than ALT) mean post-hepatic obstruction; always ask specifically about stool colour.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man in the emergency department. A sudden 30-second blackout with no warning, palpitations minutes before, quick full recovery, on metoprolol, HR 34 with cannon a waves, and an ECG showing AV dissociation with a broad infranodal escape. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute myocardial infarction causing AV block
notes: The monitor and ECG show a slow escape rhythm with no ventricular tachycardia, and he has no family history of sudden cardiac death.
He had no chest pain or breathlessness, the ECG has no ST elevation or Q waves, and the first troponin is not raised (repeat pending).
He had no prodrome (no light-headedness, sweating, pallor or visual greying), no emotional or situational trigger, and his ECG shows complete heart block.
questions.why: In transient loss of consciousness, first establish that consciousness was truly lost. Then take the history before, during and after the event, including the witness account and a question about head strike and injuries.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man in the emergency department. Fever, chills and constant diffuse abdominal pain since yesterday with ascites growing over 2 weeks, in untreated alcohol-related cirrhosis with ongoing drinking, and an ascitic neutrophil count of 1295 x10^6/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Gradual onset, no guarding or rigidity, no previous surgery, ascitic protein 9 g/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L and LDH below the serum limit, and no organisms on Gram stain.
It does not explain the fever, rigors, WCC 13.8 or the ascitic neutrophil count.
The pain is generalised, not epigastric through to the back, there is no vomiting, and lipase is 40 U/L.
questions.why: Fever, abdominal pain, worsening ascites, encephalopathy, AKI or a GI bleed in a patient with cirrhosis and ascites call for a diagnostic ascitic tap. SBP can be painless.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man in clinic. Crampy right iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea, mouth ulcers and 6 kg weight loss, with terminal ileal linear ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions, rectal sparing and a non-caseating granuloma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Colorectal cancer or small bowel lymphoma
notes: Born in Australia with no travel or TB contact, non-caseating granuloma with no acid-fast bacilli, and a negative stool pathogen PCR.
Aged 25, no palpable mass, no mass at colonoscopy and no dysplasia or malignancy on biopsy.
No rectal bleeding, terminal ileal disease, skip lesions, a normal rectum and granulomas on histology.
questions.why: Structure a procedure explanation with IPBRAD: indication, procedure (before, during, after), benefits, risks including the risk of not having it, alternatives, and documentation. Find out what the patient knows first and check understanding throughout.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman in the emergency department. Four months of exertional dyspnoea, 2-pillow orthopnoea, PND and ankle swelling a year after an anterior STEMI, with a raised JVP, S3, bibasal crackles, oedema, cardiomegaly and congestion on CXR and an NT-proBNP of 4850. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome precipitating heart failure
notes: No chest pain, a gradual 4-month course, a flat troponin (24 then 25) and an ECG unchanged from 12 months ago.
No weight loss, haemoptysis or hoarseness, and no mass or nodule on CXR.
No cough, sputum or wheeze, orthopnoea and PND with oedema, and no hyperinflation on CXR.
questions.why: Quantify breathlessness against the patient's baseline (distance, stairs or activities) and ask specifically about orthopnoea (number of pillows), PND and ankle swelling.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man in the emergency department. Fifteen years of heavy drinking, large-volume haematemesis with melaena, ascites, splenomegaly, stigmata of chronic liver disease, platelets 82, INR 1.8, albumin 27 and cirrhosis with portal hypertension on ultrasound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No weight loss, night sweats or fever and no focal liver lesion on ultrasound, with the AFP still pending.
No NSAIDs, no epigastric pain or indigestion, and only endoscopy can tell the two apart.
The blood came up without any retching or vomiting beforehand.
questions.why: In a heavy drinker with haematemesis, ascites and stigmata of chronic liver disease, treat the bleed as variceal until endoscopy proves otherwise.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man in general practice. Eight years of type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 8.9% from metformin non-adherence, gradual symmetrical stocking sensory loss to mid-shin, absent ankle reflexes, positive Romberg and loss of protective sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Spinal cord or cauda equina compression
notes: Against cord compression: no upper motor neuron signs (flexor plantars, no clonus, normal tone, knee reflexes not brisk) and no sensory level; against cauda equina: no back pain, no sphincter or saddle symptoms, and a gradual symmetrical stocking pattern rather than a saddle or radicular one.
He rarely takes the metformin, he is not vegetarian or vegan, and his B12, folate and MCV are normal.
He drinks only an occasional can of beer on weekends, and his GGT, LFTs and MCV are normal.
questions.why: Glove-and-stocking sensory loss points to a length-dependent peripheral neuropathy, a dermatomal pattern to a root or cord lesion, and a single nerve territory to a nerve compression or injury.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man in general practice. Abrupt dry cough 3 days ago with fever, malaise, fatigue, sore throat and nasal congestion, a coughing friend, no influenza vaccine this year, and influenza A detected on PCR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Cough of only 3 days with fever, no whoop or vomiting after coughing, and Bordetella pertussis not detected on PCR.
Dry cough without pleuritic pain, a clear chest, SpO2 97% on room air and RR 18.
SARS-CoV-2 not detected on PCR, with influenza A detected.
questions.why: Abrupt-onset dry cough with fever, malaise, sore throat and nasal congestion during flu season, especially with a sick contact and no vaccine this year, is influenza until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman in the emergency department. Abrupt vomiting and watery diarrhoea two days after changing her grandson's diarrhoeal nappies, temperature 37.9 °C, crampy pain eased by bowel motions and a soft abdomen with hyperactive bowel sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Pain not out of proportion, soft abdomen, sinus rhythm with no AF and lactate 1.6, although a normal lactate does not exclude it.
No blood or mucus in the stool, no high fever, no food source or travel, and a clear sick contact with a viral pattern.
No recent antibiotics or hospital stay, and a sick contact with similar symptoms.
questions.why: Acute infectious diarrhoea is diarrhoea of rapid onset lasting under 14 days. It is usually viral (norovirus in adults) and self-limiting, and rehydration is the mainstay of treatment.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man in the emergency department. Five months of progressive breathlessness with 20 kg weight loss, night sweats, blood-tinged sputum, a hoarse voice, clubbing, a hard right supraclavicular node and 50 pack-years, with a large unilateral right effusion on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: The 5-month gradual course, no pleuritic pain or sick contacts, and a normal white cell count.
Haemoptysis, a hoarse voice and a supraclavicular node point more to a primary lung cancer.
Born in Australia with no TB travel, contacts or past TB, and the smoking history and node make cancer more likely.
questions.why: In a smoker with progressive breathlessness, ask directly about weight loss, haemoptysis, hoarseness and night sweats, and quantify smoking in pack-years (20 a day for 50 years is 50 pack-years).

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man in the emergency department. Sudden chest tightness and audible wheeze after a cat and pollen exposure. He has had previous similar attacks, got partial relief from Ventolin, has had asthma since 8, both parents have asthma and he is atopic. He has widespread wheeze, raised eosinophils and hyperinflation on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No urticaria, angioedema, stridor, GI symptoms or hypotension; BP 132/80; isolated lower-airway picture typical of his previous attacks.
No pleuritic chest pain, percussion and breath sounds are equal on both sides, and the X-ray shows no pneumothorax.
No pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, leg swelling, surgery, flights or previous clots, and the widespread wheeze is explained by asthma.
questions.why: Treat first in a breathless asthmatic who cannot finish sentences: inhaled salbutamol, controlled oxygen and senior help come before the full history.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman in the emergency department. An unvaccinated traveller who ate street food, salads and ice in India, with a prodrome of fever, malaise and anorexia, RUQ pain, a tender liver, dark urine, pale stools, ALT 2840 and hepatitis A IgM detected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute cholangitis or acute calculous cholecystitis
notes: Normal platelets and spleen, a negative first antigen test and film set, and a confirmed alternative diagnosis, though 3 negative sets are still needed.
The pain is a dull constant ache rather than colic, Murphy's sign is negative, there are no gallstones and the CBD is 3 mm, and the LFTs are hepatocellular.
No epigastric pain through to the back, minimal alcohol, normal lipase and a normal pancreas on ultrasound.
questions.why: In a vomiting patient, find the cause behind the vomiting: here the prodrome, the RUQ pain and the dark urine and pale stools pointed to the liver. Patients rarely volunteer urine and stool colour, so ask.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man in the emergency department. A diabetic ex-smoker with breathlessness, chest tightness and sweating since 05:30, VF, ST elevation in V2 to V4, I, aVL, V5 and V6 with reciprocal inferior depression and Q waves, and a raised troponin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: He has no leg swelling, travel, surgery or previous clot, his rhythm was VF rather than PEA, and the ECG shows territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change.
The rise is mild, fits an acidosis of pH 7.12 after 10 minutes of arrest, and the ECG has no peaked T waves or broad QRS.
His trachea is central, air entry is equal, heart sounds are not muffled, and defibrillation restored a perfusing rhythm.
questions.why: Unresponsive and not breathing normally means cardiac arrest: call for help and start CPR at once (lower half of the sternum, 100 to 120/min, one third of chest depth, 30:2, minimal interruptions).

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man on the ward. Constant LIF pain for 3 days, a change in bowel habit, fever of 38.1 °C, LIF tenderness with localised rebound, WCC 14.6, CRP 128 and CT sigmoid wall thickening with fat stranding but no abscess or free gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No weight loss, no previous rectal bleeding or bowel change, normal Hb, no family history, and no discrete mass or enlarged nodes on CT.
Peritonism is localised with no rigidity, he is haemodynamically stable, and CT shows no collection, extraluminal gas or free gas.
No back pain or collapse, normal BP, no pulsatile mass, fever and raised markers, and an aorta of 2.1 cm on CT.
questions.why: Diverticulitis typically causes constant left iliac fossa pain with fever and a change in bowel habit. Right-sided disease is more common in patients of Asian descent.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman in general practice. Progressive solids-only dysphagia over 3 months with no difficulty initiating, 5 kg weight loss and anorexia, 15 years of GORD, obesity and 40 pack-years, and an ulcerated distal mass with adenocarcinoma in a Barrett's segment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No cough, haemoptysis or hoarseness, and no lung mass or bulky mediastinal nodes on CT.
Rapid progression with weight loss, anorexia and iron deficiency, and a malignant mass on biopsy.
The tumour is distal, within a Barrett's segment, and the histology is adenocarcinoma.
questions.why: Oropharyngeal dysphagia is difficulty starting a swallow (with choking, coughing or nasal regurgitation); oesophageal dysphagia is food sticking after the swallow.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman in the emergency department. Three weeks of constant burning forefoot pain that is worse lying flat and eased by hanging the leg, after years of claudication, with gangrene of three toes, absent right popliteal and pedal pulses, right ABI 0.28 and heavy cardiovascular risk. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of the right leg
notes: She has no new numbness or weakness, power is 5/5 and her rhythm is regular, with a stable 3-week course.
Her calves are soft, non-tender and equal with no warmth or swelling, and the pain is in the toes and eased by dependency.
The current pain is constant at rest and there is tissue loss, so she has moved beyond claudication.
questions.why: Ischaemic rest pain is constant forefoot and toe pain, worse lying flat or at night and eased by hanging the leg down. Present for more than 2 weeks, or with gangrene or an ulcer, it defines chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man on the ward. Day 5 after major orthopaedic surgery with little mobilisation, sudden pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness, HR 124, SpO2 92%, a swollen red right calf, Wells 9, and bilateral lower lobe emboli on CTPA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Sharp right-sided pleuritic pain without radiation, sweating or nausea, no ischaemic change on the ECG, and two normal troponins.
Pain is not tearing and does not go to the back, BP is equal in both arms, and the aorta is normal on CT.
No cough or sputum, a clear chest on examination and no consolidation on CT.
questions.why: Sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness after major orthopaedic surgery is PE until proven otherwise: always examine both legs for a DVT.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man in the emergency department. Breathlessness and sharp left pleuritic pain straight after a fall onto the left side, with tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins, left hyper-resonance and reduced breath sounds, tachycardia, hypotension, hypoxia, and complete left lung collapse with mediastinal shift on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Heart sounds are not muffled, the trachea is deviated, and the left chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds on one side; a normal cardiac silhouette does not exclude acute tamponade, so eFAST is still needed.
The left chest is hyper-resonant rather than dull, the X-ray shows no effusion or fluid level, the neck veins are distended rather than flat, and the Hb is normal.
No leg swelling, immobility, travel or previous clots, and the trauma and one-sided signs explain the picture.
questions.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: breathlessness, hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and hyper-resonance with reduced or absent breath sounds. Decompress before imaging.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy in the emergency department. Acute expiratory wheeze with recession over a few hours after a 2-day cold, a partial response to salbutamol, rhinovirus on PCR, smoke exposure, day-care, preterm birth and atopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: There was no choking episode, the wheeze is bilateral and symmetrical, and it followed a coryzal illness.
No urticaria, angioedema, vomiting or floppiness, no new food or sting, and the onset was gradual after a cold.
He has no wheeze or night cough between colds and no other triggers, and at 3 years episodic viral wheeze is more likely.
questions.why: In a wheezy preschool child, always ask about anaphylaxis (skin signs with another system involved, new foods, stings) and an inhaled foreign body (sudden choking), because both need different, urgent treatment.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man in the emergency department. Two weeks of worsening breathlessness with orthopnoea, PND and pink frothy sputum a month after an MI, 2 weeks of regular ibuprofen, a raised JVP, S3 and crackles, NT-proBNP 8400 and a chest X-ray showing alveolar oedema, upper lobe diversion and effusions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No chest pain, nausea or radiation, and the ECG is unchanged from his discharge ECG.
No pleuritic pain, calf swelling or immobility, and orthopnoea, PND, an S3 and oedema on X-ray explain the picture.
No fever or purulent sputum, normal WCC, only a small CRP rise, and the change is bilateral with upper lobe diversion and effusions.
questions.why: Ask every breathless patient about orthopnoea (how many pillows), PND, frothy pink sputum and exercise tolerance, and examine the JVP, heart sounds for an S3, lung bases and ankles.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman in the emergency department. Constant right upper quadrant pain for over 24 hours after a fatty meal, with right shoulder radiation, fever to 38.9, a positive Murphy's sign, WCC 14.2, CRP 96, and an ultrasound showing a 5 mm wall, pericholecystic fluid and a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute coronary syndrome or right lower lobe pneumonia
notes: No clinical jaundice, bilirubin only 26, common bile duct 5 mm with no intrahepatic dilatation, and normal BP and lactate.
No chest pain, breathlessness or cough, chest clear including the right base, SpO2 97% on room air, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST or T wave changes.
This pain has been constant and worsening for over a day, with fever, raised WCC and CRP, and a thickened gallbladder wall.
questions.why: Biliary colic is postprandial pain that settles within about 6 hours. Constant RUQ pain for hours, with fever, Murphy's sign and raised WCC and CRP, is acute cholecystitis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman in the emergency department. Sudden colicky periumbilical pain, early large bilious vomiting, no stool or flatus for 3 days, mild distension and tinkling bowel sounds after two caesarean sections and an appendicectomy, with dilated small bowel and a collapsed colon on X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Strangulated or closed-loop small bowel obstruction
notes: The pain is still colicky, she is afebrile with no guarding or rebound, and the lactate is normal.
The hernial orifices and scars are normal with no cough impulse.
Distension is mild, the vomiting was early, large and bilious, and the colon is collapsed on X-ray.
questions.why: Colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation are the cardinal features of bowel obstruction. Always ask specifically about flatus and previous abdominal surgery.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man in the emergency department. He shared needles 2 months ago, had a prodrome of fever, arthralgia, urticaria and malaise, now has jaundice with dark urine and pale stools and a tender smooth liver, with ALT 1635 and HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc and HBeAg positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Paracetamol or other drug-induced liver injury
notes: No rigors, haemodynamically stable, normal WCC with only a mild CRP rise, transaminase rise far greater than the ALP rise, a viral prodrome, and no duct dilatation or stones on ultrasound.
He denies any paracetamol, overdose, other medicines or supplements, and the paracetamol level is undetectable.
The HCV antibody is negative, although this can be falsely reassuring in the window period, and the hepatitis B serology already explains the illness.
questions.why: Viral hepatitis has a prodrome (anorexia, malaise, fever, RUQ pain; urticaria and arthralgia especially in hepatitis B), then an icteric phase with dark urine, pale stools, itch and jaundice.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man in the emergency department. He takes ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with aspirin, rarely takes his PPI, has months of nocturnal epigastric pain eased by food, haematemesis with 2 weeks of melaena, a fall in Hb from 138 to 84 and a urea of 16.8. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Bleeding peptic ulcer related to NSAID and aspirin use
notes: Only one spider naevus with no other stigmata, no ascites or splenomegaly, and normal platelets, INR, albumin and bilirubin.
The abdomen is soft and not distended with normal bowel sounds and no rigidity, and the erect chest X-ray shows no free gas.
Erosive disease rarely causes a bleed large enough to drop the Hb by more than 50 g/L with haemodynamic change.
questions.why: In upper GI bleeding, decide three things early: stable or unstable, variceal or non-variceal, and major or minor (Glasgow-Blatchford score). Each changes the management.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman in general practice. Returned from Thailand a month ago after eating street food without pre-travel vaccination, with a 2-week prodrome, then jaundice, a hepatocellular picture and a positive HAV IgM. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: No gallstones or bile duct dilatation on ultrasound, ALT far higher than ALP, and a normal white cell count.
Normal haemoglobin and platelets, and a positive HAV IgM explains the picture.
Constant pain not related to food, no history of gallstones, and no stones or duct dilatation on ultrasound.
questions.why: Dark urine and pale stools mean conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Always ask the 4 Ps (pee, poo, pruritus, pain) in jaundice.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman in the emergency department. RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad), pale stools, dark urine and itch, cholestatic LFTs with WCC 17.8 and CRP 186, and an 11 mm common bile duct with a distal stone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Lipase 42 is normal, the pain does not go through to the back, and the visualised pancreas is normal.
She is jaundiced with obstructive features, Murphy's sign is negative, and the gallbladder wall is thin with no pericholecystic fluid.
No IV drugs, travel or unsafe sex, the LFTs are cholestatic with ALP and GGT raised more than ALT, and the bile ducts are dilated.
questions.why: RUQ pain, fever with rigors and jaundice (Charcot's triad) is acute cholangitis until proven otherwise. Confusion and hypotension (Reynolds' pentad) mean severe disease.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl in the emergency department. Type 1 diabetes with doses skipped to lose weight, HbA1c 9%, thirst, polyuria, weight loss, vomiting, Kussmaul breathing, glucose 22, ketones 5.3 and a high anion gap acidosis with pH 7.25. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by insulin omission
notes: No headache, bradycardia, hypertension, pupil change or focal signs; pCO2 appropriately compensated (no excess hypocapnia); drowsiness can come from the DKA itself. But her effective osmolality is normal (2 × 128 + 22 = 278 mOsm/kg) and her acidosis is only moderate, so a GCS of 13 is not fully explained: treat as possible cerebral oedema and reassess the GCS hourly.
She is afebrile with no neck stiffness or rash, the CRP is normal, and DKA explains the drowsiness.
She was home all evening, no tablets are missing, and the glucose, ketones and gas explain her conscious state.
questions.why: Check a glucose and ketones in every vomiting or drowsy child with diabetes. Be cautious about diagnosing gastroenteritis when there is vomiting without diarrhoea; look for another cause. DKA can be the first presentation of type 1 diabetes.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man on the ward. Ischaemic chest pain and palpitations just before a witnessed collapse, a troponin rising from 46 to 2850 ng/L, lateral ST depression and VF on the strip. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: He is on therapeutic enoxaparin, his chest pain was ischaemic rather than pleuritic, and the rhythm is VF rather than PEA.
Rupture usually occurs days after infarction and presents with PEA, not VF, and his haemoglobin is normal.
The strip shows chaotic deflections of varying amplitude with no organised QRS complexes.
questions.why: In an unresponsive patient, slow noisy gasps are not normal breathing, and a few seconds of jerking at collapse is usually hypoxic jerking, not a seizure. Start compressions straight away; do not wait for a pulse check.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man in the emergency department. Two days of worsening headache with fever, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia and positive Kernig's sign in a man on prednisolone, with turbid neutrophilic CSF, high protein and a low glucose ratio. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: He is oriented with GCS 15, intact attention, no drowsiness, behaviour change, seizures or focal signs.
It was not a thunderclap or worst-ever, with no collapse, and has built over 2 days with fever; the CT is normal and the CSF has minimal red cells.
His CSF is turbid with neutrophils, a high protein and a low glucose, and he has a CRP of 214 with a raised lactate.
questions.why: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean meningitis until proven otherwise. Always ask about and look for a non-blanching rash.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman in general practice. Fever of 39 °C, a worsening generalised headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and a positive Kernig's sign in an 18-year-old after a crowded festival with a shared tent and uncertain meningococcal vaccination; the CSF is neutrophilic with a low glucose, Gram-negative diplococci and a positive N. meningitidis PCR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: She is alert and oriented (GCS 15) with no seizures, behaviour change or focal signs, and the CSF is neutrophilic with organisms seen.
The headache built up over hours, she has a fever and a coryzal prodrome, and the CSF has no xanthochromia and only 5 red cells.
The CSF has 8500 neutrophils, a protein of 1.1 g/L, a glucose ratio of 0.24 and Gram-negative diplococci.
questions.why: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia mean bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. Ask about and look for a rash, but its absence does not exclude meningococcal disease.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman in general practice. Five stereotyped attacks of severe, one-sided throbbing headache lasting 6 to 7 hours, with light and noise sensitivity and nausea, each preceded by about 20 minutes of fully reversible visual aura, with a normal examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: The onset was gradual, it is the same as four previous attacks, and the neurological examination and fundi are normal.
She is afebrile, with no neck stiffness, negative Kernig's sign and no rash.
The visual symptoms are positive (dots, jumbled lines), spread gradually, resolve fully and are followed by headache, with no weakness, numbness or speech change and a normal examination.
questions.why: Ask how fast the headache started and whether it matches previous attacks. A gradual, stereotyped headache with a normal examination and no red flags (SNOOP) needs no imaging.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man in general practice. Two months of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with LIF pain, weight loss, fatigue and erythema nodosum, and continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 25 cm with crypt distortion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
notes: Age 25, and colonoscopy found no mass, with no dysplasia on biopsy.
Continuous inflammation from the rectum, normal terminal ileum, inflammation confined to the mucosa, no granulomas and no perianal disease.
No travel, sick contacts or antibiotics, a 2-month course, and negative stool PCR, culture, C. difficile and parasite tests.
questions.why: Chronic bloody, mucousy diarrhoea with weight loss in a young adult is inflammatory bowel disease until proven otherwise; IBS cannot be diagnosed with blood, weight loss, nocturnal stools or a raised calprotectin.
